'''Hamilton Othanel Smith''' (August 31, 1931 – October 25, 2025) was an American [[microbiologist]] and Nobel laureate.<ref name="Gitschier 2012">{{Cite journal | last1 = Gitschier | first1 = J. | title = A Half-Century of Inspiration: An Interview with Hamilton Smith | doi = 10.1371/journal.pgen.1002466 | journal = [[PLOS Genetics]]| volume = 8 | issue = 1 | article-number = e1002466 | year = 2012 | pmid =  22253610| pmc = 3257296 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>Multiple sources:

==Early life and education==
Hamilton Othanel Smith was born in [[New York City]] on August 31, 1931<ref name = birthplace>{{cite web  |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1978/smith/facts/
|title = Hamilton O. Smith Facts}}</ref><ref name = deathplace>{{cite web |title=Remembering Hamilton O. Smith |url=https://www.jcvi.org/media-center/remembering-hamilton-o-smith |website=J. Craig Venter Institute |date=October 2025 |access-date=28 October 2025}}</ref> and grew up in Urbana-Champaign, Illinois.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Venter |first=J. Craig |date=2025-11-10 |title=Hamilton Smith obituary: molecular biologist who co-discovered precise molecular scissors for cutting DNA |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q136779436 |journal=Nature |volume=647 |issue=8089 |pages=311–311 |doi=10.1038/D41586-025-03635-Y}}</ref>

Smith graduated from [[University Laboratory High School of Urbana, Illinois]]. He attended the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]], but in 1950 transferred to the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he earned his [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] in Mathematics in 1952.  He received his medical degree from [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]] in 1956.<ref name=":0" /> Between 1956 and 1957 Smith worked for the [[Washington University in St. Louis]] Medical Service. 

During the next few years he undertook US Navy military service as well as a medical residency at [[Henry Ford Hospital]].<ref name=":0" /> Hamilton then went to the [[University of Michigan in Ann Arbor]] on a US [[National Institutes of Health]] fellowship where he worked with infectious disease expert [[Myron M. Levine]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1975, he was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] he spent at the [[University of Zurich]].

==Scientific career==
In 1970, Smith and Kent W. Wilcox discovered the first type II [[restriction enzyme]],<ref>{{Cite journal | author = Smith H, Wilcox KW | title = A Restriction enzyme from Hemophilus influenzae *1I. Purification and general properties | journal = [[Journal of Molecular Biology]] | volume = 51 | issue = 2 | pages = 379–391 | year = 1970 | pmid = 5312500 | doi = 10.1016/0022-2836(70)90149-X}}</ref> which is now known as HindII.<ref name="Gitschier 2012"/> Smith went on to discover DNA [[methylase]]s that constitute the other half of the bacterial host restriction and modification systems, as hypothesized by [[Werner Arber]] of Switzerland.<ref name="Gitschier 2012"/>

Smith was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] in 1978 for discovering type II [[restriction enzyme]]s with [[Werner Arber]] and [[Daniel Nathans]] as co-recipients.

He later became a leading figure in the nascent field of [[genomics]], when in 1995 he and a team at [[The Institute for Genomic Research]] sequenced the first [[bacteria]]l [[genome]], that of ''[[Haemophilus influenzae]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=1330118|year=1992|last1=Smith|first1=H. O.|title=A restriction enzyme from Hemophilus influenzae. I. Purification and general properties. 1970|journal=Biotechnology (Reading, Mass.)|volume=24|pages=38–50|last2=Wilcox|first2=K. W.}}</ref> ''H. influenza'' was the same organism in which Smith had discovered restriction enzymes in the late 1960s.  He subsequently played a key role in the sequencing of many of the early genomes at The Institute for Genomic Research, and in the assembly of the [[human genome]] at [[Celera Genomics]], which he joined when it was founded in 1998.

Smith later directed a team at the [[J. Craig Venter Institute]] that worked towards creating a partially [[synthetic biology|synthetic]] bacterium, ''[[Mycoplasma laboratorium]]''. In 2003 the same group synthetically assembled the genome of a virus, [[Phi X 174]] [[bacteriophage]]. Smith was scientific director of privately held [[Synthetic Genomics]], which was founded in 2005 by [[Craig Venter]] to continue this work. Synthetic Genomics is working to produce [[biofuel]]s on an industrial-scale using recombinant [[algae]] and other microorganisms.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.xconomy.com/san-diego/2009/06/04/craig-venter-has-algae-biofuel-in-synthetic-genomics-pipeline/|title=Craig Venter Has Algae Biofuel in Synthetic Genomics' Pipeline - Xconomy|work=Xconomy|date=4 June 2009 }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Smith was married to Liz Smith until her death and they had five children.<ref name = deathplace/> They also had 12 grandchildren and 15 great grandchildren. One son preceded him in death.<ref name = deathplace/>

Smith was diagnosed with [[lymphoma]] in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2020/12/19/after-saving-countless-lives-nobel-laureate-hamilton-smith-retires-as-his-own-health-falters/|title=After saving countless lives, Nobel laureate Hamilton Smith retires as his own health falters|publisher=San Diego Tribune|accessdate=October 29, 2025|date=December 19, 2020}}</ref> He died at his home in [[Ellicott City, Maryland]], on October 25, 2025, at the age of 94.<ref name = deathplace/><ref>{{Cite news |last=Ricks |first=Delthia |date=2025-12-05 |title=Hamilton O. Smith, Who Made a Biotech Breakthrough, Is Dead at 94 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/05/science/hamilton-smith-dead.html |access-date=2026-05-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>
